---
title: "Quiz: image formation and the PSF"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Notation: PSF = image of a point, OTF = its Fourier transform, NA = numerical aperture, λ = wavelength.

---

**Q1.** Why is the image of a fluorescent sample a **sum** of PSFs, one per point of the object, weighted by its brightness?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Do the light waves from two different molecules interfere?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Fluorescent molecules emit independently (incoherent light), so their waves do not interfere on average: the **intensities** add. Each point contributes a copy of the PSF, scaled by its brightness and shifted to its position. A weighted sum of shifted copies of one kernel is a convolution: image = object ∗ PSF.
:::

---

**Q2.** A grating of period 300 nm is imaged with an NA 1.4 objective at 520 nm. The OTF at that frequency is 0.27. What does the image of the grating look like?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The OTF multiplies the contrast of each stripe pattern.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The same stripes, same period and position, with 27 % of the original contrast: a pattern $1 + \cos$ becomes $1 + 0.27\cos$. The mean brightness is unchanged ($H(0) = 1$).
:::

---

**Q3.** Which improves the resolution more: halving the wavelength, or doubling the NA?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Look at $0.61\lambda/\mathrm{NA}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Both halve $0.61\lambda/\mathrm{NA}$: the same improvement. In practice neither is free: NA is limited to about 1.4–1.5 (it cannot exceed the refractive index of the immersion medium), and the wavelength is set by the fluorescent dye.
:::

---

**Q4.** A grating of period 150 nm lies under an NA 1.4 objective (λ = 520 nm). Is it blurred, or is it gone? Would a better camera help?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Compare its frequency with $2\mathrm{NA}/\lambda$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Its frequency, 6.7 cycles/µm, is above the cut-off $2 \cdot 1.4/0.52 = 5.4$ cycles/µm. The OTF is exactly zero there: the grating does not reach the camera at all, so the image is the same as without the grating. No camera can record what the lens did not pass.
:::

---

**Q5.** In a defocused image of a striped test pattern, one band of stripes appears **inverted** (dark where the pattern is bright). Why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does a negative OTF value do to $1 + \cos$?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The OTF of a defocused lens becomes **negative** at some frequencies. A stripe pattern at such a frequency is imaged as $1 + H\cos$ with $H < 0$: the stripes are shifted by half a period, bright and dark swap. Stripes at other frequencies keep their sign.
:::

---

**Q6.** A camera moved by 2 µm (in the sample plane) along $x$ during the exposure. Which stripe patterns along $x$ vanish completely?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The OTF of a line of length $L$ is a sinc with zeros at $k/L$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Those with frequencies $1/L, 2/L, \dots$ = 0.5, 1, 1.5, … cycles/µm along $x$, i.e. periods 2 µm, 1 µm, 667 nm, …: each such stripe is averaged over exactly a whole number of periods. Stripes along $y$ (frequency in $y$ only) are not affected.
:::

---

**Q7.** The Gaussian approximation of the PSF uses $\sigma = 0.21\lambda/\mathrm{NA}$. What does it get right, and what does it miss?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Compare the profile and the OTF of the two.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It matches the central disc: almost the same width (FWHM 0.49 against 0.51 λ/NA) and almost the same OTF at low and middle frequencies. It misses the **rings** of the Airy pattern and the **hard cut-off**: a Gaussian OTF is never exactly zero, so it pretends that very fine detail passes a little.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Show that a PSF normalised to $\int h(\mathbf x)\,d\mathbf x = 1$ has $H(\mathbf 0) = 1$, and say what that means for the image.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Put $\mathbf k = 0$ into the Fourier integral.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$H(\mathbf k) = \int h(\mathbf x)\,e^{-2\pi i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}\,d\mathbf x$, so $H(\mathbf 0) = \int h(\mathbf x)\,d\mathbf x = 1$. Frequency 0 is the mean brightness (the total light): blur redistributes the light but does not change its total.
:::

---

**Q9.** *(math)* Why is the OTF of a perfect lens zero beyond $2\mathrm{NA}/\lambda$, and not beyond $\mathrm{NA}/\lambda$, the radius of the pupil?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The intensity PSF is $|a|^2$; what is the Fourier transform of a product?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The amplitude PSF $a$ contains frequencies up to $\mathrm{NA}/\lambda$ (the pupil). The intensity $h = a\,a^*$ is a product, so its spectrum is the autocorrelation of the pupil: the overlap of the disc with a shifted copy, non-zero for shifts up to the disc's **diameter**, $2\mathrm{NA}/\lambda$.
:::
